newsitem.title: FRANCE: OECD takes aim at European grain export taxes.
newsitem.headline: OECD takes aim at European grain export taxes.

text.p: The European Union came under fire from the OECD on Thursday for slapping taxes on grain exports.

The international free-market organisation added its own voice to criticism from the U.S. and some of Europe's own farmers, who say the taxes are unfair, distort trade and may harm developing countries.
"Export restrictions and taxes are distorting measures and potentially disruptive of trade," the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development said in an annual farm review.
"Moreover resort to such measures may contribute to the anxiety concerning food security of countries heavily dependent on food imports," it said.
The European Union put taxes on wheat and barley exports last year when alarm over low stocks pushed world prices above the level paid to EU farmers for the first time in 20 years.
The taxes, replacing subsidies traditionally handed out to farmers to help them compete when world prices are lower, were meant to maintain supplies and protect consumers at home.
But the U.S. objected to the taxes as a market distortion and the row is simmering again now that Brussels has taxed wheat once more to halt exports until the new harvest.
EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler last month defended the taxes as a logical consequence of world prices that had begun rising again after falling steeply from last year's record.
But France, which tried to block the wheat tax in May, argues it is unnecessary because prices have headed lower yet again, preventing its farmers from competing without subsidies.
The EU last week reduced the tax from 15 Ecus a tonne to five Ecus, but has so far avoided going back to subsidy.

A decision on marketing next season's crop, to be harvested from July, is expected at the end of June. EU officials have said export subsidies will then be inevitable to bridge the gap with lower U.S. wheat prices, but that for now Brussels is right to be cautious until recent drought damage can be assessed.
The OECD said its criticism applied to a number of countries that restricted exports in last year's price boom, but a passage on the EU made it plain Brussels was mainly at fault.
Measures such as the EU taxes "mask market signals and may disrupt trade," it said.

It also repeated a warning from last year's annual report that EU farmers were being over-compensated for cuts in official support prices because the actual price they were getting on the market was higher than the price on which payments were set.
In general, however, it said consumers in the 15-nation bloc had benefited from a switch to direct payments and away from market support, which the OECD blames for driving up food costs.
